claims.source: Recently, de novo variants in TRPM3 were reported in patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), including 16 patients with the recurrent missense variant p.Val1002Met and two additional patients with the variants p.Pro1102Gln and p.Ser1367Thr, respectively (de Sainte Agathe et al., 2020; Dyment et al., 2019; Gauthier et al., 2021; Kang et al., 2021; Lines et al., 2022; see results and Figure 1 for further discussion and details on numbering of TRPM3 variants).
claims.evidence: This is based on previously published case reports cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Patients with TRPM3 variants consistently present with moderate-to-severe GDD and ID, variably associated with other clinical features such as childhood-onset epilepsy, hypotonia, altered heat, and/or pain sensitivity and variable facial dysmorphism.
claims.source: These patients consistently present with moderate-to-severe GDD and ID, variably associated with other clinical features such as childhood-onset epilepsy, hypotonia, altered heat, and/or pain sensitivity and variable facial dysmorphism.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical observations from previously reported patients.

claims.claim: Functional characterization of the p.Val1002Met and p.Pro1102Gln variants in heterologous expression systems indicated that both lead to a gain of channel function.
claims.source: Functional characterization of the p.Val1002Met and p.Pro1102Gln variants in heterologous expression systems indicated that both lead to a gain of channel function (Van Hoeymissen et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on previously published functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The large majority of TRPM3 transcripts in human cerebellum use exon 2 as first exon (85%).
claims.source: This analysis indicates that the large majority of transcripts in human cerebellum use exon 2 as first exon (85%), have a short pore loop (>98%), and do not undergo intron retention in exon 28 (82%).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis from human cerebellum shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: More than 98% of TRPM3 transcripts in human cerebellum have a short pore loop.
claims.source: This analysis indicates that the large majority of transcripts in human cerebellum use exon 2 as first exon (85%), have a short pore loop (>98%), and do not undergo intron retention in exon 28 (82%).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis from human cerebellum shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: 82% of TRPM3 transcripts in human cerebellum do not undergo intron retention in exon 28.
claims.source: This analysis indicates that the large majority of transcripts in human cerebellum use exon 2 as first exon (85%), have a short pore loop (>98%), and do not undergo intron retention in exon 28 (82%).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis from human cerebellum shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: A TRPM3 construct using exon 2 as the start exon, with a short pore, including all three optional exons as well as the full exon 28 (transcript variant NM_001366147.2) did not yield a functional channel upon heterologous expression in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: A construct using exon 2 as the start exon, with a short pore, including all three optional exons as well as the full exon 28 (transcript variant NM_001366147.2), corresponding to a protein of 1744 amino acids, did, however, not yield a functional channel upon heterologous expression in HEK293T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A TRPM3 construct lacking exon 8 (transcript NM_001366145.2) yielded robust TRPM3-dependent signals upon expression in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: In contrast, a construct lacking the lowly expressed exon 8 (transcript NM_001366145.2) yielded robust TRPM3-dependent signals upon expression in HEK293T cells, as assessed using Fura-2-based calcium microfluorimetry and whole-cell patch-clamp experiments.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Eight individuals carried a de novo TRPM3 variant, while one male patient had inherited the variant from his mildly affected father.
claims.source: Eight individuals carried a de novo variant, while one male patient had inherited the variant from his mildly affected father.
claims.evidence: This is based on genetic testing and family history data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: The first symptoms in patients with TRPM3 variants were observed within the first year of life in 8 out of 10 patients.
claims.source: The first symptoms were observed within the first year of life in 8 out of 10 patients and included hypotonia, poor visual contact or pursuit, and motor delay.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical history data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Gross motor milestones were delayed in 9 out of 10 patients with TRPM3 variants.
claims.source: Gross motor milestones were delayed in 9 out of 10 patients, autonomous walking was achieved late, between 19 and 25 months in 4 out of 10 patients, walking with aid in one patient at 4 years, and walking was not achieved in 4 out of 10 patients (ages 21 months, 3 years, 10 years, and 20 years at time of study).
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical assessment data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Four patients with TRPM3 variants had cerebellar ataxia.
claims.source: Four patients had cerebellar ataxia, and two other patients showed severe hypotonia without weakness and with nystagmus that may be related to cerebellar involvement.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical examination data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Language development was normal in 3 out of 10 patients with TRPM3 variants, delayed in 3 patients, and absent in 4 patients.
claims.source: Language development was normal in 3 out of 10 patients, delayed in 3 patients, and absent in 4 patients.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical assessment data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Intellectual deficiency was observed in all subjects with TRPM3 variants, ranging from a low normal-mildly reduced IQ in 3 out of 10 patients to severe intellectual deficiency in 4 patients.
claims.source: Intellectual deficiency was observed in all subjects, ranging from a low normal-mildly reduced IQ in 3 out of 10 patients to severe intellectual deficiency in 4 patients.
claims.evidence: This is based on neuropsychological assessment data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Epilepsy was diagnosed in only two patients with TRPM3 variants.
claims.source: Epilepsy was diagnosed in only two patients: one patient had nocturnal generalized tonic-clonic seizures since 7 years of age, and a further patient had electrical status epilepticus during slow-wave sleep (ESES).
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical and EEG data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Seven out of 10 patients with TRPM3 variants showed skeletal anomalies.
claims.source: Notably, 7 out of 10 patients showed skeletal anomalies: hip subluxation (Wagner et al., 2008), patellar dislocation (Vriens et al., 2011), Perthes' disease (Vriens et al., 2011), brachydactyly (Vriens et al., 2011), valgus foot (Wagner et al., 2008), and rib hypoplasia (Vriens et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical examination and imaging data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Five out of 8 patients with TRPM3 variants showed cerebellar atrophy on cranial MRI.
claims.source: Cranial MRI was normal in 3 out of 8 patients. However, a substantial number of patients showed cerebellar atrophy (5 out of 8 patients): vermian and cerebellar hemispheres atrophy in patients n° 1–4 (Figure 2 and Table 1) and a localized partial atrophy of both cerebellar hemispheres in patient n° 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on MRI imaging data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Serial cranial MRI performed in three patients showed that the cerebellar atrophy was progressive and was not present in MRI performed in the first months of life.
claims.source: Serial cranial MRI performed in three patients showed that the atrophy was progressive and was not present in MRI performed in the first months of life (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on longitudinal MRI data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Four out of 10 patients with TRPM3 variants exhibit pain insensitivity.
claims.source: Finally, 4 out of 10 patients exhibit pain insensitivity, and 2 patients showed heat insensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical assessment data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Two patients with TRPM3 variants showed heat insensitivity.
claims.source: Finally, 4 out of 10 patients exhibit pain insensitivity, and 2 patients showed heat insensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical assessment data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: All seven novel TRPM3 variants were absent from the gnomAD database.
claims.source: All variants were absent from the gnomAD database and predicted to be pathogenic according to at least two out of four prediction meta-analysis programs like REVEL (CADD, DANN, and PROVEAN; Table 3; Quang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on database searches and computational predictions.

claims.claim: All seven novel TRPM3 variants were predicted to be pathogenic according to at least two out of four prediction meta-analysis programs.
claims.source: All variants were absent from the gnomAD database and predicted to be pathogenic according to at least two out of four prediction meta-analysis programs like REVEL (CADD, DANN, and PROVEAN; Table 3; Quang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational pathogenicity predictions.

claims.claim: The disease-associated TRPM3 variants are located in highly conserved areas across orthologs from multiple species.
claims.source: Sequence alignment at positions D614, L769, V1002, G1007, P1102, N1126, and S1133 shows that the variants are located in highly conserved areas, both across orthologs from multiple species (Drosophila, zebrafish, mouse, rat, and macaca) and in the most closely related homologs within the TRPM subfamily, namely TRPM1, TRPM6, and TRPM7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Many of the disease-associated TRPM3 variants cluster at the interface between the transmembrane domain and the cytosol.
claims.source: When mapped on the recent cryo-EM structure of TRPM3 in the closed state and in the presence of Gβγ (pdb:8DDQ; Zhao and MacKinnon, 2023), it can be noted that many of the disease-associated variants cluster at the interface between the transmembrane domain and the cytosol (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural mapping using cryo-EM structure data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Residue D614 is located in a cytosolic loop that is disordered in the cryo-EM structures, just adjacent to the TRPM3-Gβγ interaction site.
claims.source: Interestingly, residue D614 is located in a cytosolic loop that is disordered in the cryo-EM structures. In the structure of the TRPM3 channel subunit in contact with nanobody-tethered Gβγ (pdb:8DDQ), D614 is located just adjacent to the TRPM3-Gβγ interaction site (Behrendt et al., 2020; Zhao and MacKinnon, 2023) raising the possibility that charge neutralization in the D614V variant may affect Gβγ-dependent channel regulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis using cryo-EM structure data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Charge neutralization in the D614V variant may affect Gβγ-dependent channel regulation.
claims.source: Interestingly, residue D614 is located in a cytosolic loop that is disordered in the cryo-EM structures. In the structure of the TRPM3 channel subunit in contact with nanobody-tethered Gβγ (pdb:8DDQ), D614 is located just adjacent to the TRPM3-Gβγ interaction site (Behrendt et al., 2020; Zhao and MacKinnon, 2023) raising the possibility that charge neutralization in the D614V variant may affect Gβγ-dependent channel regulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and location of the variant.

claims.claim: Cells transfected with wild-type TRPM3 showed a small increase in basal intracellular calcium concentration compared to non-transfected cells.
claims.source: In line with earlier work, cells transfected with the WT TRPM3 construct showed a small increase in basal intracellular calcium concentration ([Ca2+]i) compared to non-transfected (NT) cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: In wild-type TRPM3 transfected cells, the cytosolic calcium concentration decreased slightly in response to treatment with 100 µM primidone.
claims.source: In WT transfected cells, the cytosolic [Ca2+]i decreased slightly in response to treatment with a high dose of primidone (100 µM; Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: All newly identified TRPM3 variants, with the exception of the L769V variant, exhibited basal calcium levels that were significantly higher compared to non-transfected cells or cells transfected with wild-type TRPM3.
claims.source: When overexpressing the newly identified TRPM3 variants, with the exception of the L769V variant, we consistently observed basal [Ca2+]i levels that were significantly higher compared to NT cells or cells transfected with WT-TRPM3, an effect that was most pronounced for the V1002G variant (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Application of primidone caused a reduction of intracellular calcium in cells expressing TRPM3 variants, except for the L769V and the G1007S variant.
claims.source: Except for the L769V and the G1007S variant, application of primidone caused a reduction of [Ca2+]i, albeit not to the levels of NT cells (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: PS responses were increased for the D614V, N1126D, and S1133P variants compared to wild-type TRPM3.
claims.source: Compared to WT-TRPM3, PS responses were increased for the D614V, N1126D, and S1133P variants and reduced for the L769V, V1002G, V1002L, and G1007S variants (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: PS responses were reduced for the L769V, V1002G, V1002L, and G1007S variants compared to wild-type TRPM3.
claims.source: Compared to WT-TRPM3, PS responses were increased for the D614V, N1126D, and S1133P variants and reduced for the L769V, V1002G, V1002L, and G1007S variants (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Significantly higher basal calcium levels were observed for all wild-type/variant mixtures compared to cells expressing only wild-type TRPM3, with the exception of the P1102Q and N1126D variant.
claims.source: Under these conditions, significantly higher basal [Ca2+]i levels for all WT/variant mixtures were observed compared to cells expressing only WT-TRPM3, with the exception of the P1102Q and N1126D variant, where the elevated basal [Ca2+]i levels were found not to be significant.
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments with co-transfection of wild-type and variant TRPM3.

claims.claim: Under heterozygous conditions, primidone caused a reduction in basal calcium for all tested variants with higher basal calcium levels.
claims.source: Moreover, under these heterozygous conditions, primidone caused a reduction in basal [Ca2+]i for all tested variants with higher basal [Ca2+]i levels (Figure 4A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Cells co-expressing wild-type TRPM3 with any of the newly discovered disease-associated variants consistently exhibited larger PS-induced calcium responses.
claims.source: Finally, cells co-expressing WT-TRPM3 with any of the newly discovered disease-associated variants consistently exhibited larger PS-induced Ca2+ responses (Figure 4C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Cells expressing wild-type plus L769V, G1007S, and wild-type plus G1007S produced robust outwardly rectifying currents.
claims.source: We observed that cells expressing WT + L769 V, G1007S, and WT + G1007 S produced robust outwardly rectifying currents, whereas currents in cells expressing only L769V were not different from those in NT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on whole-cell patch-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Currents in cells expressing only L769V were not different from those in non-transfected cells.
claims.source: We observed that cells expressing WT + L769 V, G1007S, and WT + G1007 S produced robust outwardly rectifying currents, whereas currents in cells expressing only L769V were not different from those in NT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on whole-cell patch-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Upon stimulation with PS, robust outwardly rectifying currents were evoked in cells expressing wild-type, wild-type plus L769V, G1007S, and wild-type plus G1007S.
claims.source: Upon stimulation with PS, robust outwardly rectifying currents were evoked in cells expressing WT, WT + L769 V, G1007S, and WT + G1007 S, whereas currents in cells expressing L769V were not different from those in NT controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on whole-cell patch-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: In cells expressing wild-type plus L769V, an increase in inward current at –160 mV was measured when compared to non-transfected controls.
claims.source: Notably, in cells expressing WT + L769V, we measured an increase in inward current at –160 mV when compared to NT controls, reminiscent of the inwardly rectifying current component observed in the V1002M variant (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E; Van Hoeymissen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on whole-cell patch-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The concentration-response curve for PS was shifted to lower concentrations for the heterozygous G1007S condition, but not for the homozygous condition.
claims.source: These experiments revealed a shift of the concentration-response curve to lower PS concentrations for the heterozygous, but not for the homozygous condition (EC50 value of 2.9±0.3 µM, 4.0±0.5 µM, and 1.1±0.1 µM for, respectively, WT-TRPM3, homozygous G1007S, and heterozygous WT + G1007 S transfected HEK293 cells; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on dose-response experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: All patient variants are dominant gain-of-function mutations, provoking significantly increased basal activity resulting in cellular calcium overload, as well as enhanced PS-induced responses.
claims.source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that all patient variants are dominant gain-of-function mutations, provoking significantly increased basal activity resulting in cellular calcium overload, as well as enhanced PS-induced responses.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined experimental data from calcium imaging and electrophysiology.

claims.claim: For variants V1002L, G1007S, N1126D, and S1133P, YFP levels were not higher than in cells expressing wild-type TRPM3.
claims.source: For variants V1002L, G1007S, N1126D, and S1133P, YFP levels were not higher than in cells expressing WT-TRPM3, similar to our earlier observations for the V1002M and P1102Q variants (Van Hoeymissen et al., 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on YFP fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: In cells expressing the L769V variant in the absence of wild-type subunits, cellular YFP values were significantly reduced compared to wild-type.
claims.source: In cells expressing the L769V variant in the absence of WT subunits, which do not show a response to the channel antagonist primidone or the channel agonist PS (Figure 3), cellular YFP values were significantly reduced compared to WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on YFP fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Normal YFP levels were found in cells co-expressing the L769V variant with wild-type TRPM3.
claims.source: However, normal YFP levels were found in cells co-expressing the L769V variant with WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on YFP fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: In the case of D614V and V1002G variants, cellular YFP levels were significantly higher than wild-type control, both under homozygous and heterozygous conditions.
claims.source: Finally, in the case of D614V and V1002G variants, cellular YFP levels were significantly higher than WT control, both under homozygous and heterozygous conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on YFP fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: In cells with similar YFP fluorescence, basal calcium levels were consistently higher for cells expressing the D614V and V1002G variants, either alone or with wild-type subunits.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that, in cells with similar YFP fluorescence, basal [Ca2+]i levels were consistently higher for cells expressing the D614V and V1002G variants, either alone or with WT subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of YFP fluorescence and calcium levels shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Elevated basal calcium levels in cells expressing disease-associated TRPM3 variants can be attributed to increased activity of individual channels rather than to increased channel protein expression.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that elevated basal [Ca2+]i levels in cells expressing disease-associated TRPM3 variants can be attributed to increased activity of individual channels rather than to increased channel protein expression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined YFP fluorescence and calcium imaging data.

claims.claim: TRPM3 is robustly expressed in different cell types of the developing and adult cerebellum and adult cortex.
claims.source: By reanalyzing publicly available single cell RNA sequencing datasets of the developing (Aldinger et al., 2021) and adult (Lake et al., 2018) cerebellum and adult cortex (Velmeshev et al., 2019), it becomes apparent that TRPM3 is robustly expressed in different cell types of these brain regions (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on reanalysis of published single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Highest expression of TRPM3 in the adult cortex was found in layer 5/6 neurons.
claims.source: Highest expression of TRPM3 in the adult cortex (Velmeshev et al., 2019) was found in layer 5/6 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, C, E).
claims.evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: TRPM3 expression was observed in distinct cellular clusters of the adult cerebellum, including neuronal and non-neuronal cell types.
claims.source: Furthermore, TRPM3 expression was observed in distinct cellular clusters of the adult cerebellum (Lake et al., 2018), including neuronal (e.g. distinct cerebellar granule cells and Purkinje neurons) and non-neuronal (e.g. cerebellar-specific astrocytes) cell types (Figure 5B, D and F).
claims.evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Prominent TRPM3 expression was observed in early stages of the developing cerebellum.
claims.source: Interestingly, prominent TRPM3 expression was observed in early stages of the developing cerebellum (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, D) and detected in different cell types (Figure 5A, C and E), including excitatory cerebellar and unipolar brush cell interneurons, and Purkinje cells (Aldinger et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Highest TRPM3 expression in the developing cerebellum is noted in cells of the rhombic lip.
claims.source: Highest expression is noted in cells of the rhombic lip (Figure 5A, C, E and G), where TRPM3 is expressed in all four zones: choroid plexus epithelium, intermediate zone, subventricular zone, and ventricular zone (Aldinger et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Low TRPM3 RNA levels were detected in different muscle types.
claims.source: Interestingly, low RNA levels were detected in different muscle types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq tissue data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Hypotonia in most of the patients is most likely caused by malfunctioning of the neuronal innervation of the skeletal muscles, probably related to a cerebellar defect.
claims.source: This might suggest that hypotonia in most of the patients (Table 1) is most likely caused by malfunctioning of the neuronal innervation of the skeletal muscles, probably related to a cerebellar defect.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the low TRPM3 expression in muscle and high expression in cerebellum.

claims.claim: The expression data of TRPM3 in the CNS points toward an important role of the channel in specific brain regions, both in the early developmental and adult stage.
claims.source: Taken together, the expression data of TRPM3 in the CNS points toward an important role of the channel in specific brain regions, both in the early developmental and adult stage.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression data analysis.

claims.claim: Cerebellar atrophy could be progressive in patients with TRPM3 variants who have a clinically non-progressive disorder.
claims.source: As it is known in some other congenital ataxia, we observed that cerebellar atrophy could be progressive in a patient who has a clinically non-progressive disorder.
claims.evidence: This is based on longitudinal MRI observations in the patient cohort.

claims.claim: The p.(Gly1007Ser) variant is associated with a milder phenotype.
claims.source: Although clinical variability, even intra-familial, is observed with the same mutation, we point on some possible genotype-phenotype correlation to be confirmed in larger series, with p.(Gly1007Ser) being associated with a milder phenotype and p.(Asn1126Asp) with a more severe phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical observations from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: The p.(Asn1126Asp) variant is associated with a more severe phenotype.
claims.source: Although clinical variability, even intra-familial, is observed with the same mutation, we point on some possible genotype-phenotype correlation to be confirmed in larger series, with p.(Gly1007Ser) being associated with a milder phenotype and p.(Asn1126Asp) with a more severe phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical observations from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: The cerebellum is known to integrate neuronal networks coupling motor function with cognition, emotional skills, and language.
claims.source: The cerebellum is known to integrate neuronal networks coupling motor function with cognition, emotional skills, and language (Leto et al., 2016; Sathyanesan et al., 2019; Schmahmann, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar function supported by citations.

claims.claim: Distortion of cerebellar development could induce cerebellar diseases.
claims.source: Distortion of cerebellar development could induce (cerebellar) diseases (Sathyanesan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The different disease-associated gain-of-function variants occur in different parts of the TRPM3 channel, suggesting that they increase channel activity via distinct mechanisms.
claims.source: The different disease-associated gain-of-function variants occur in different parts of the TRPM3 channel, including the cytosolic N-terminus, the transmembrane region, and the cytosolic C-terminus, suggesting that they increase channel activity via distinct mechanisms (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural location of the variants.

claims.claim: Increased protein expression levels can be excluded as an underlying mechanism for increased channel activity of disease-associated variants.
claims.source: Based on fluorescent tagging of the channels, we can exclude increased protein expression levels as an underlying mechanism, suggesting that the variants affect channel gating or membrane localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on YFP fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The affected residues L769, V1002, G1007, N1126, and S1133 cluster at the interface between the transmembrane domain and the cytosol, in a region critically involved in the gating of TRPM3 and related channels.
claims.source: In this respect, it is interesting to note that when mapped on the recent cryo-EM structure of TRPM3, the affected residues L769, V1002, G1007, N1126, and S1133 cluster at the interface between the transmembrane domain and the cytosol, in the gating of TRPM3 and related channels with six transmembrane domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Owsianik et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural mapping and inference about functional significance.

claims.claim: The p.(Val1002Met) variant showed a reduced sensitivity toward Gβγ-dependent modulation compared to wild-type transfected cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, our previous results showed a reduced sensitivity toward Gβγ-dependent modulation for the p.(Val1002Met) variant compared to WT transfected cells (Van Hoeymissen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on previously published experimental data.

claims.claim: There are known mutations in GNB1 causing severe neurodevelopmental disability, hypotonia, and seizures.
claims.source: Interestingly, there are known mutations in the upstream genetic component guanine nucleotide-binding protein beta 1 (GNB1) causing severe neurodevelopmental disability, hypotonia, and seizures (Petrovski et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited reference.

claims.claim: Mutations in GNB2 and GNB5 are observed in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders.
claims.source: In addition, other mutations in GNB2 (Fukuda et al., 2020) and GNB5 (Lodder et al., 2016) are observed in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from cited references.

claims.claim: Neurodevelopmental phenotypes associated with GNB mutations could be partially explained via dysregulation of downstream TRPM3 activity.
claims.source: Potentially, these neurodevelopmental phenotypes could be partially explained via dysregulation of downstream TRPM3 activity.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known interaction between Gβγ and TRPM3.

claims.claim: L769V was the only variant that exhibited no functional activity when expressed in the absence of wild-type channel subunits, whereas it caused a gain-of-function in the presence of wild-type subunits.
claims.source: Notably, L769V was the only variant that exhibited no functional activity when expressed in the absence of WT channel subunits, whereas it caused a gain-of-function in the presence of WT subunits, which corresponds to the situation in the cells of the heterozygous patients.
claims.evidence: This is based on functional characterization experiments.

claims.claim: The variation in the N-terminus (L769V) may affect proper trafficking of the homotetrameric channel to the plasma membrane, and this trafficking deficit can be rescued by heteromeric channels composed of wild-type and variant subunits.
claims.source: One possible explanation could be that the variation in the N-terminus affects proper trafficking of the homotetrameric channel to the plasma membrane and that this trafficking deficit can be rescued by heteromeric channels composed of WT and variant subunits.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed functional data for L769V.

claims.claim: The increased channel activity under basal conditions and associated increased basal calcium levels observed with all the characterized disease-associated TRPM3 variants can be blocked by application of a high dose of primidone.
claims.source: Importantly, the increased channel activity under basal conditions and associated increased basal calcium levels observed with all the characterized disease-associated TRPM3 variants can be blocked by application of a high dose of the antiepileptic drug primidone, which has been identified as a direct TRPM3 antagonist in in vitro studies and in animal models (Krügel et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data showing the effect of primidone on mutant channels.

claims.claim: Plasma levels in subjects taking primidone are expected to be sufficiently high to cause significant inhibition of TRPM3 activity.

claims.claim: Increased channel activity, potentially leading to neuronal hyperexcitability and cellular calcium overload, underlies a spectrum of TRPM3 channelopathies.
claims.source: The disease-associated variants consistently result in a pronounced gain of channel function, providing strong support for the hypothesis that increased channel activity, potentially leading to neuronal hyperexcitability and cellular calcium overload, underlies a spectrum of TRPM3 channelopathies.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined clinical and functional data.

results.result: Ten patients carrying seven novel heterozygous TRPM3 missense variants were identified, presenting with a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental symptoms including global developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, musculo-skeletal anomalies, altered pain/heat perception, and notably, a cerebellar phenotype with ataxia or severe hypotonia, nystagmus, and progressive cerebellar atrophy in more than half of patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C35 provide comprehensive clinical characterization of 10 patients with detailed phenotypic data including motor milestones, cognitive assessments, neurological findings, and MRI evidence of cerebellar atrophy. The data are systematically presented in Table 1 and Figure 2, with longitudinal MRI demonstrating progressive cerebellar atrophy. The clinical observations are well-documented and internally consistent.

results.result: All seven novel TRPM3 variants are absent from gnomAD, predicted pathogenic by multiple algorithms, located in highly conserved regions across species, and cluster at the interface between the transmembrane domain and cytosol in the TRPM3 structure, with D614V positioned adjacent to the Gβγ interaction site.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by database searches (gnomAD), computational predictions (Table 3), sequence alignment analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and structural mapping using cryo-EM data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The structural localization provides mechanistic insight, though C41 regarding D614V affecting Gβγ regulation remains speculative.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis of human cerebellum reveals that the majority of TRPM3 transcripts use exon 2 as first exon (85%), have a short pore loop (>98%), and do not undergo intron retention in exon 28 (82%). A construct lacking exon 8 (NM_001366145.2) yields functional channels, while one including exon 8 (NM_001366147.2) does not.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 are based on RNA-seq data analysis from human cerebellum (Figure 1A) and functional validation experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The splice variant analysis is quantitative and the functional characterization using calcium imaging and patch-clamp provides clear evidence for differential functionality of splice variants.

results.result: When expressed alone in HEK293T cells, all newly identified TRPM3 variants except L769V exhibited significantly elevated basal calcium levels compared to wild-type, with most variants showing reduction upon primidone treatment. Pregnenolone sulfate responses were increased for D614V, N1126D, and S1133P variants but reduced for L769V, V1002G, V1002L, and G1007S variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 are supported by calcium imaging experiments (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1-2) with appropriate controls (non-transfected and wild-type). Statistical analyses are provided with p-values, and data are from at least 3 independent experiments. The mixed PS responses suggest variant-specific mechanisms, which is acknowledged.

results.result: Under heterozygous conditions (1:1 co-expression of wild-type and variant TRPM3), all variants except P1102Q and N1126D showed significantly elevated basal calcium levels. Primidone reduced basal calcium for all variants with elevated levels, and all variants consistently exhibited larger pregnenolone sulfate-induced calcium responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by co-transfection experiments (Figure 4, Figure 3—figure supplements 1-2, Figure 4—figure supplements 1-2) that model the patient heterozygous condition. The data demonstrate dominant gain-of-function effects with appropriate statistical analysis. This is critical evidence linking variants to disease mechanism.

results.result: Patch-clamp electrophysiology revealed that L769V alone produces no functional currents, but co-expression with wild-type yields robust outwardly rectifying currents and an increased inward current component. G1007S shows functional currents both alone and with wild-type, with the heterozygous condition exhibiting a leftward shift in pregnenolone sulfate concentration-response curve.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by whole-cell patch-clamp experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) with appropriate voltage protocols and dose-response analysis. The L769V data reveal a unique trafficking-dependent mechanism, while G1007S shows enhanced agonist sensitivity in the heterozygous state. Statistical comparisons are provided.

results.result: All patient variants are dominant gain-of-function mutations causing increased basal activity and cellular calcium overload, with elevated calcium levels attributed to increased channel activity rather than increased protein expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C56 and C62 represent integrative conclusions supported by the combined calcium imaging, electrophysiology, and YFP fluorescence data (C42-C61). The YFP analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) controls for expression levels, demonstrating that gain-of-function is due to altered channel properties rather than increased expression for most variants.

results.result: YFP fluorescence measurements reveal that most variants (V1002L, G1007S, N1126D, S1133P) show normal expression levels, L769V shows reduced expression alone but normal with wild-type co-expression, while D614V and V1002G show increased expression. When normalized for expression, D614V and V1002G still exhibit higher basal calcium levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by YFP fluorescence measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) with appropriate normalization and statistical analysis. The analysis of basal calcium versus YFP fluorescence for individual cells provides strong evidence that gain-of-function is not simply due to increased expression, particularly for D614V and V1002G.

results.result: Reanalysis of single-cell RNA-seq datasets reveals robust TRPM3 expression in different cell types of developing and adult cerebellum and adult cortex, with highest expression in layer 5/6 cortical neurons, cerebellar granule cells, Purkinje neurons, and cells of the rhombic lip in developing cerebellum. Low expression was detected in muscle types.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 are supported by reanalysis of published single-cell RNA-seq datasets (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2) from multiple sources (Aldinger et al. 2021, Lake et al. 2018, Velmeshev et al. 2019). The expression patterns are visualized through UMAP plots and dot plots showing cell-type specificity and developmental stages.

results.result: The expression data suggest that hypotonia in patients is likely caused by malfunctioning neuronal innervation of skeletal muscles related to cerebellar defects, and TRPM3 plays an important role in specific brain regions during both developmental and adult stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 represent inferences from expression data. While C68 shows low TRPM3 expression in muscle and C63-C67 show high cerebellar expression, the causal link to hypotonia (C69) is speculative without functional studies. C70 is a reasonable inference but requires validation through functional experiments in relevant brain regions.

results.result: Cerebellar atrophy can be progressive in patients with clinically non-progressive disorder. Possible genotype-phenotype correlations suggest p.(Gly1007Ser) is associated with milder phenotype and p.(Asn1126Asp) with more severe phenotype, though these require confirmation in larger series.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by longitudinal MRI data (Figure 2, C33). However, C72-C73 regarding genotype-phenotype correlations are based on limited patient numbers (3 patients with G1007S, 2 with N1126D) and show clinical variability even within families. The authors appropriately note these correlations need confirmation in larger cohorts.

results.result: Disease-associated variants occur in different parts of TRPM3 (N-terminus, transmembrane, C-terminus) suggesting distinct mechanisms. Increased protein expression is excluded as the mechanism, and affected residues L769, V1002, G1007, N1126, and S1133 cluster at the transmembrane-cytosol interface in a region critical for gating.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 are supported by structural mapping (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), YFP expression data (C57-C61), and functional characterization showing variant-specific effects. The structural clustering provides mechanistic insight, though the exact mechanisms for each variant remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: L769V exhibits no functional activity when expressed alone but causes gain-of-function with wild-type subunits. This may be explained by the N-terminus variation affecting trafficking of homotetrameric channels, with the deficit rescued by heteromeric channels.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is strongly supported by functional data (C51-C52, C58-C59). Claim C84 is a reasonable mechanistic hypothesis based on the trafficking pattern and YFP data, though it remains speculative without direct trafficking experiments. The hypothesis is appropriately presented as a possibility requiring further investigation.

results.result: Primidone blocks increased basal channel activity and calcium levels in all disease-associated variants. Plasma levels in subjects taking primidone are expected to be sufficient for TRPM3 inhibition, warranting evaluation of whether primidone can alleviate symptoms in patients.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is supported by experimental data (C9, C43, C45, C49). Claim C86 is based on pharmacokinetic knowledge and reasonable inference. Claim C87 is appropriately framed as a proposal for future clinical evaluation rather than an established therapeutic benefit. The therapeutic potential is supported by mechanism but requires clinical validation.

results.result: Gain-of-function of TRPM3 causes a spectrum of autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorders with frequent cerebellar involvement. TRPM3 should be added to NGS panels for epilepsy, ID, and congenital ataxia diagnosis. Increased channel activity leading to neuronal hyperexcitability and calcium overload underlies TRPM3 channelopathies.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C88, and C89 represent the main conclusions integrating clinical (C4-C35), genetic (C36-C41), and functional (C42-C56) data. The evidence strongly supports gain-of-function as the disease mechanism and the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. The recommendation for NGS panel inclusion (C88) is justified by the clinical findings. The mechanistic model (C89) is well-supported by the functional data.

results.result: Background information establishing TRPM3 as a temperature- and neurosteroid-sensitive channel expressed in various tissues including CNS, with prior reports of de novo variants in patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy showing gain-of-function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C13-C18 represent established knowledge and prior work appropriately cited from the literature. These provide essential context for the current study and are well-supported by the cited references.

results.result: Background on cerebellar function, prior findings on V1002M variant's reduced Gβγ sensitivity, and known GNB mutations causing neurodevelopmental disorders, with speculation that GNB phenotypes could involve TRPM3 dysregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75, C79-C81 represent established knowledge appropriately cited. Claim C82 is appropriately framed as speculation about potential mechanistic links between GNB mutations and TRPM3, based on known interactions but requiring experimental validation.

results.result: TRPM3 antagonists are supported as potential therapy for TRPM3-related disorders.
results.evaluation: Claim C11 is supported by the primidone data (C9, C85) showing effective blockade of mutant channel activity. However, this represents a therapeutic hypothesis requiring clinical validation. The support is mechanistic rather than clinical, which is appropriately acknowledged in the manuscript.
